questions.title: Split a dataset into train, validation, and test sets
questions.prompt: Write Python code using scikit-learn's train_test_split to split a dataset into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% test, and explain why you need all three rather than just a train/test split.
questions.code: # X, y already loaded as arrays/DataFrames
questions.modelAnswer: A three-way split exists because the training set teaches the model, but you still need a separate set to make decisions about the model while building it (which hyperparameters, which features, when to stop training) -- that's the validation set's job. If you tuned those decisions directly against the test set, the test set would stop being a trustworthy, unbiased final check, since you'd have indirectly fit decisions to it. The test set is reserved and touched only once, at the very end, to report a final, honest estimate of how the model performs on genuinely unseen data. train_test_split only does a two-way split per call, so getting three sets means calling it twice: first splitting off the test set, then splitting the remainder into train and validation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd call train_test_split twice: first splitting off the test set at 15% of the total, with a fixed random_state for reproducibility, then splitting the remaining 85% again so train and validation end up at roughly 70% and 15% of the original total respectively. The reason I keep validation and test strictly separate, rather than just using one holdout set for everything, is that I'm going to look at validation performance repeatedly while tuning the model -- trying different settings and checking how each one does -- and if I used the test set for that same tuning loop, I'd eventually be fitting my choices to it indirectly, which defeats its whole purpose as a final, unbiased check I only look at once, at the very end.
questions.example:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# First split off the test set (15%)
X_train_val, X_test, y_train_val, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.15, random_state=42
)

# Then split the remainder into train (70% of total) and validation (15% of total)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_train_val, y_train_val, test_size=0.1765, random_state=42
)
commonMistakes: Using only a train/test split and tuning hyperparameters directly against the test set
Forgetting train_test_split only splits two ways per call, requiring two calls for a three-way split
Not using a fixed random_state, making the split (and therefore results) non-reproducible between runs
Miscalculating the second split's test_size fraction, resulting in uneven final proportions
keyPoints: Training set teaches the model; validation set is used for tuning decisions during development; test set is a final, untouched check
Tuning against the test set directly would make it an unreliable, biased final estimate
train_test_split does a two-way split per call -- call it twice for a three-way split
The test set should be touched only once, at the very end

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct code producing a 70/15/15 split
Correctly explains why validation and test must be separate
Mentions reproducibility (random_state)

questions.title: Debugging a pip dependency conflict
questions.prompt: Running pip install some-ai-library fails with an error saying it requires a different version of a package you already have installed, which is also required by another library you need. How do you diagnose and resolve this?
questions.modelAnswer: pip's error message in this situation names the specific conflicting requirement -- read it carefully first, since it will say exactly which package and version range is incompatible with what's already installed, rather than guessing. The real fix in almost every case is isolation, not forcing a version: create a fresh virtual environment (python -m venv) dedicated to this project so its dependencies don't have to coexist with every other project's dependencies in one global environment, which is very often why the conflict exists in the first place -- it's not that the two libraries are fundamentally incompatible with each other, it's that they're being forced to share one global installation alongside unrelated packages with their own separate requirements. If the conflict persists even inside a clean, isolated environment, that's a genuine incompatibility between the two specific libraries, and the real options are checking each library's documentation for a compatible version pin, or accepting that they may not currently be usable together in the same environment.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always to actually read the conflict message pip prints, since it names the specific package and version ranges at odds, rather than jumping straight to blindly forcing a different version. My second move is almost always isolation: am I even inside a dedicated virtual environment for this project, or am I installing into some shared global Python that has a dozen unrelated projects' dependencies piled into it? Most of the dependency conflicts I've hit in practice go away the moment I create a clean venv just for this project, because the 'conflict' was really just two unrelated projects' requirements colliding in one shared installation, not a genuine incompatibility between the two libraries themselves. If the conflict still happens inside a brand-new, otherwise-empty venv, then it's a real incompatibility, and I'd check each library's release notes for a version combination that's documented to work together.
questions.example:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows
pip install some-ai-library
# retry inside a clean, isolated environment before assuming it's a genuine incompatibility
commonMistakes: Jumping to force-reinstalling or ignoring the requirement before reading what the conflict message actually says
Installing into a shared global Python environment instead of a project-specific virtual environment
Assuming the conflict means the two libraries can never work together, without first testing inside a clean environment
Not pinning working versions in requirements.txt once a compatible combination is found, risking the same conflict resurfacing later
keyPoints: Read pip's conflict message carefully -- it names the specific incompatible requirement
Most dependency conflicts stem from a shared global environment, not a genuine library incompatibility
A fresh, isolated virtual environment resolves most of these conflicts outright
If the conflict persists in a clean environment, it's genuine and needs a documented compatible version combination

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the likely cause (shared environment)
Proposes isolation via a fresh virtual environment as the fix
Distinguishes a genuine incompatibility from an environment problem

questions.title: Debugging the mutable default argument bug
questions.prompt: A function def add_item(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items is called repeatedly with just one argument each time, and the returned list keeps growing across unrelated calls instead of starting fresh each time. What's actually happening, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: A default parameter value is evaluated exactly once, at the moment the function is defined -- not fresh on every call -- so items=[] creates a single list object that becomes the default for every call that doesn't explicitly supply its own items argument. Because that one list object is shared across all those calls, appending to it in one call leaves the appended item there for the next call too, making it look like the list is accumulating across unrelated calls, when really there's just one underlying list being mutated repeatedly. The standard fix is to use None as the actual default and create a new list inside the function body when needed: default items to None, then at the top of the function body check if items is None and assign items = [] -- this guarantees a brand-new list is created fresh on every call that doesn't supply its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as one of Python's most famous gotchas: the items=[] in the signature only runs once, when Python first reads the def statement, not every time the function is called. So every call that relies on the default is secretly sharing the exact same list object behind the scenes, and anything appended in one call is still sitting there the next time, since nothing ever created a fresh empty list in between. I'd fix it with the standard pattern: give items a default of None instead of [], then at the top of the function body write a check that creates a new list only if items is still None -- now a genuinely new, empty list gets created every single time the function runs without an explicit items argument, instead of reusing one shared list across every call.
questions.example:
# BUG
def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add_item('a'))  # ['a']
print(add_item('b'))  # ['a', 'b'] -- unexpected! same shared list

# FIXED
def add_item(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items
commonMistakes: Not realizing a default parameter value is evaluated once at definition time, not fresh per call
Using a mutable default ([], {}, or set()) at all instead of None plus a None-check inside the function
Assuming this is a bug in Python itself rather than a well-known, documented gotcha with a standard fix
Fixing it by reassigning items = [] unconditionally at the top, which breaks the case where a caller deliberately passes their own items list
keyPoints: Default parameter values are evaluated once, at function definition time
A mutable default is shared across every call that doesn't override it, causing it to persist/accumulate
The standard fix: default to None, then create a new mutable object inside the function body if it's still None
Never use a mutable literal ([], {}, set()) directly as a default parameter value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why the default is shared across calls
Provides the correct None-default fix
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: A blocking call stalls an async function
questions.prompt: You write an async function meant to call three AI APIs concurrently with asyncio.gather, but inside each coroutine you use the plain, synchronous requests.get() instead of an async HTTP client, and the three calls end up running one after another instead of concurrently. Why does that happen, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: async/await and asyncio.gather only achieve real concurrency when every potentially slow operation inside the coroutines actually yields control back to the event loop while it waits -- that's what await does. requests.get() is a synchronous, blocking call: it doesn't know anything about asyncio's event loop, so when it's waiting on a network response, it blocks the entire thread, including the event loop that's supposed to be free to run the other two coroutines in the meantime. The result is that even though the code is technically wrapped in async def and gathered with asyncio.gather, the three requests.get() calls still happen one after another, because each one fully occupies the thread until it personally finishes, exactly like they would without asyncio involved at all. The fix is to replace the blocking call with a genuinely async-aware HTTP client, such as httpx's AsyncClient with an awaited get call, which does properly hand control back to the event loop while waiting on the network, letting the other coroutines actually run during that wait.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that writing async def around a function doesn't automatically make everything inside it concurrent -- it only works if what's inside also knows how to cooperate with the event loop, and requests.get() just doesn't; it's a plain blocking call that monopolizes the thread until the network response comes back, full stop. So even inside an asyncio.gather of three coroutines, if each coroutine's real work is a requests.get() call, the three calls still run strictly one after another, because each fully blocks the only thread doing the work before the next one gets a chance to even start. The fix is swapping requests for an async-native client like httpx and awaiting the client's get call inside an async context manager -- now the await genuinely yields control back to the event loop during the network wait, which is exactly what lets the other two coroutines actually make progress at the same time.
questions.example:
# BROKEN: looks concurrent, actually runs sequentially
async def fetch(url):
    return requests.get(url)  # blocking call, doesn't yield to the event loop

# FIXED: genuinely concurrent
async def fetch(url):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        return await client.get(url)  # yields control while waiting
commonMistakes: Assuming wrapping code in async def automatically makes blocking calls inside it non-blocking
Using a synchronous library (requests) inside an async function instead of an async-native one (httpx, aiohttp)
Not noticing the symptom -- calls completing one after another despite using asyncio.gather -- as a sign of a hidden blocking call
Mixing sync and async HTTP clients inconsistently across a codebase instead of standardizing on one async client for concurrent code
keyPoints: async/await only achieves concurrency if every slow operation inside genuinely yields to the event loop
requests.get() is synchronous/blocking and doesn't cooperate with asyncio at all
A blocking call inside an async function silently serializes what should be concurrent work
Fix: use an async-native client (httpx.AsyncClient, aiohttp) with await for genuinely concurrent I/O

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the blocking-call root cause
Explains why asyncio.gather alone doesn't fix it
Provides the correct async-client fix

questions.title: Recovering from a detached HEAD state
questions.prompt: You run git checkout on an old commit hash to look at some old code, make a couple of commits while exploring, and then realize Git has been warning you about a 'detached HEAD' the whole time. What does that actually mean, and how do you recover your new commits without losing them?
questions.modelAnswer: Normally HEAD points at a branch name, and a branch name moves forward automatically with each new commit. Checking out a specific commit hash instead of a branch name puts HEAD directly on that commit -- detached from any branch -- so any new commits made in that state still get created, but nothing is tracking or advancing a branch pointer to include them; they exist, but they're not reachable from any branch. The real risk is that if you simply check out a branch again without first doing something about those commits, they become effectively orphaned, unreachable from any branch name, and eventually eligible for Git's garbage collection. The fix is to create a new branch right at the detached commit before switching away: git branch new-branch-name (or git switch -c new-branch-name), which gives those otherwise-orphaned commits a real branch name pointing at them, making them permanently reachable again.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I notice the detached HEAD warning, before I do anything else, I'd run git branch recovered-work right where I am -- that creates a brand-new branch pointing at exactly the commit I'm currently sitting on, including whatever I've committed since detaching. That one command is the entire fix: it takes commits that were about to become unreachable the moment I switched to another branch, and gives them a permanent home. I'd specifically avoid just checking out main first and trying to figure it out after, because at that point the commits are still technically findable with git reflog for a while, but it's a much more stressful recovery than just branching from where I already am before switching away.
questions.example:
# Oops -- already on a detached HEAD after a couple commits
git branch recovered-work   # points a new branch at the current (detached) commit
git checkout recovered-work # now safely on a real branch with those commits

# If you already switched away: git reflog can help locate the orphaned commit hash
commonMistakes: Switching to another branch before creating a new branch to capture the detached commits, risking orphaning them
Panicking and assuming the commits are permanently lost rather than recoverable via git branch or git reflog
Not understanding that new commits CAN be made in a detached HEAD state -- they just aren't tracked by any branch
Confusing a detached HEAD with an actual error; Git allows it deliberately for inspecting old history
keyPoints: Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly at a commit, not at a branch name
Commits made in a detached HEAD state exist but aren't reachable from any branch
Create a new branch at the current commit (git branch <name>) before switching away, to keep the commits reachable
git reflog is a fallback to recover an already-orphaned commit hash if you switched away too soon

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what detached HEAD means
Correctly explains the risk of losing the commits
Provides the correct recovery fix (branch at the current commit)

questions.title: You just committed an API key
questions.prompt: You accidentally commit a file containing a real AI provider API key and push it to a shared GitHub repository. You catch it a few minutes later. What do you actually need to do, in order, and why isn't simply deleting the file in a new commit enough?
questions.modelAnswer: Deleting the file in a new commit only removes it from the current, latest snapshot of the repository -- the commit that actually added the key is still sitting in the repository's history, fully intact and retrievable by anyone with access to the repo (or anyone who already pulled or cloned it before the fix), so the key is still fully exposed even after the 'fix' commit. The first and most urgent action, before anything about Git itself, is rotating the key -- going to the AI provider's dashboard and revoking the leaked key, generating a new one -- because once a secret has been pushed anywhere outside your own machine, you have to assume it's compromised and treat removing it from history as a cleanup step, not the actual fix. After rotating the key, cleaning the history itself (with tools like git filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner, or simply accepting it if the repo is small and early enough to just start history over) is worth doing for hygiene, but it is not a substitute for rotating the key, since anyone who already has a copy of the repo still has the old key regardless of what later happens to history.
questions.professionalAnswer: My very first move, before touching Git again at all, is going straight to the AI provider's dashboard and revoking that key, then generating a replacement. That's non-negotiable and has to happen immediately, because the instant that commit was pushed, I have to assume the key is compromised -- someone could have already seen it, scraped it, or cloned the repo in those few minutes. Only after the key is dead do I worry about cleanup: deleting the file in a new commit is fine for keeping the current state of the repo clean going forward, but I'm clear that it does nothing about the actual exposure, since the original commit with the real key is still sitting in history, fully retrievable by anyone who looks. If the repo and its history matter enough, I'd use a tool like git filter-repo to actually scrub the key out of every historical commit, but I treat that as hygiene on top of an already-rotated key, never as the fix itself.
commonMistakes: Deleting the file in a new commit and assuming that resolves the exposure
Rotating the key only after trying to clean up Git history, instead of rotating it first and immediately
Not realizing anyone who already pulled or cloned the repo still has the old commit with the key regardless of later history cleanup
Treating this as purely a Git problem instead of first and foremost a security incident requiring key rotation
keyPoints: The original commit with the key is still fully present in history even after a later deletion commit
Rotate (revoke and replace) the leaked key immediately -- this is the actual fix, not an optional extra step
History cleanup (filter-repo, BFG) is hygiene on top of rotation, not a substitute for it
Anyone who already cloned/pulled the repo before the fix still has the old key regardless of later history changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why deleting the file alone is insufficient
Identifies key rotation as the immediate, non-negotiable first step
Mentions history cleanup as a secondary hygiene step

questions.title: A pull request's CI check is failing
questions.prompt: You open a pull request and GitHub shows a red X next to a check called 'run-tests'. How would you investigate what actually failed, and what are the most common beginner-level reasons a check like this fails that have nothing to do with your actual feature logic?
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is simply opening the failing check's details/logs directly from the pull request page -- GitHub shows the full output of whatever command the workflow ran, and that log almost always names the specific failing test or error near the end of the output, rather than requiring guesswork. Common beginner-level causes that have nothing to do with the actual feature's logic include: a missing or outdated dependency in requirements.txt that the CI environment doesn't have, since CI builds a clean environment from scratch rather than reusing whatever happens to already be installed on your own machine; an environment variable or secret the code expects that isn't configured in the CI environment; a test that passes locally but relies on something environment-specific, like a particular file path or time zone, that differs in CI; and simply not having run the test suite locally before pushing, so a straightforward, easily-caught failure only surfaces once CI runs it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd click straight into the failing check's log rather than guessing, since GitHub Actions shows the full command output and the actual error or failing test name is almost always right there near the bottom. A few things I check first because they're the most common beginner trip-ups: did I actually add a new dependency to requirements.txt, or does it just happen to already be installed on my own machine locally; is there an environment variable or secret my code reads that simply isn't set up in the CI environment the same way it is on my machine; and, honestly, did I actually run the test suite locally before pushing at all, because a huge fraction of 'mystery' CI failures are just a test I'd have caught in ten seconds if I'd run it myself first. Once I've read the actual log and ruled those out, I treat it like any other test failure -- reproduce it, fix the actual code, and push again to re-trigger the check.
commonMistakes: Not opening the actual failing check's logs and instead guessing at what might be wrong
Forgetting CI builds a clean environment from scratch, so a locally-installed-but-unlisted dependency works locally but fails in CI
Assuming environment variables/secrets available locally are automatically available in the CI environment
Pushing without ever running the test suite locally first, letting an easily-caught failure show up only in CI
keyPoints: Open the failing check's actual log output first -- the specific failure is almost always named there
Missing dependencies in requirements.txt are a common cause, since CI builds a clean environment
Missing environment variables/secrets in the CI environment is another common cause
Run the test suite locally before pushing to catch easily-avoidable failures earlier

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes checking the actual CI logs as the first investigation step
Names at least two realistic beginner-level, non-logic causes
Clarity of the overall investigation approach

questions.title: Handling a 429 Too Many Requests response
questions.prompt: Your code is calling an AI provider's API in a loop and starts getting back 429 Too Many Requests responses partway through. What's actually happening, and how should your code handle it instead of just failing or hammering the API with immediate retries?
questions.modelAnswer: A 429 means the API is deliberately rejecting the request because the caller has exceeded a rate limit -- a cap on how many requests (or how many tokens) are allowed within a given time window -- it's not a sign the request itself was malformed or wrong. Retrying immediately in a tight loop makes the situation strictly worse: it keeps sending requests that will keep getting rejected, and can push the account further into a penalty or even trigger a longer cooldown. The correct handling is exponential backoff: on a 429, wait before retrying, and increase that wait time with each consecutive failure (for example doubling it), ideally also reading the Retry-After header if the API provides one, which tells you exactly how long to wait rather than guessing. Adding a small amount of random jitter to the wait time also helps when multiple processes are hitting rate limits at the same time, so they don't all retry at exactly the same moment and immediately re-trigger the limit together.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd first make sure the code actually distinguishes a 429 from other errors rather than treating every failure the same way, since a 429 specifically means 'you're going too fast,' not 'something is broken.' My handling is a backoff loop: catch the 429, check for a Retry-After header and use that wait time if it's present, otherwise fall back to an exponential backoff starting around a second and doubling on each consecutive 429, up to some sane maximum. I'd also add a little random jitter to that wait so that if several workers in a batch job all hit the limit at once, they don't all wake up and retry in the exact same instant, instantly re-triggering the limit together. What I'd specifically avoid is a tight retry-immediately loop, which just hammers an API that's already telling me to slow down.
commonMistakes: Retrying immediately in a tight loop on a 429 instead of backing off
Treating a 429 the same as a generic error instead of recognizing it specifically means 'rate limited'
Ignoring a Retry-After header when the API actually provides one
Not adding jitter, causing multiple concurrent callers to retry in sync and immediately re-trigger the limit
keyPoints: 429 means the rate limit was exceeded -- the request itself wasn't malformed
Immediate tight-loop retries make the situation worse and risk a longer penalty
Use exponential backoff, respecting a Retry-After header if provided
Add jitter to avoid multiple callers retrying in sync

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a 429 means
Correctly describes exponential backoff as the fix
Mentions Retry-After and/or jitter

questions.title: Debugging a JSON decode error from an API response
questions.prompt: Your code calls response.json() on an API response and it raises a JSON decode error, even though the request appeared to succeed. What are the most likely causes, and how would you investigate before assuming the API itself is broken?
questions.modelAnswer: response.json() fails whenever the response body isn't actually valid JSON, which happens more often than it sounds like it should, for a few common reasons: the request actually failed (an error status code) but the error body is HTML or plain text, not JSON -- so the problem isn't really a JSON bug at all, it's a missed status-code check before trying to parse; the response is empty (zero-length body), which isn't valid JSON either, often from a request that technically got through but returned no content; or, less commonly, the response is a streaming or paginated format that isn't meant to be parsed as one single JSON document at all. The investigation sequence is: print or log response.status_code and the raw response.text (not response.json()) first to see exactly what actually came back, before assuming the parser itself is broken -- in the large majority of cases, the raw text reveals an HTML error page, an empty body, or a plain-text error message instead of the JSON that was expected.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd even consider the JSON parser itself broken, I'd print response.status_code and response.text -- the raw, unparsed text -- to actually see what came back. Nine times out of ten, that reveals the real problem: maybe the status code is 502 and the body is an HTML error page from a load balancer or gateway, not JSON at all, in which case the actual bug is that I never checked the status code before calling .json() on an error response. Or the body is just completely empty, which also fails to parse as JSON. I treat 'JSON decode error' as a symptom pointing at something upstream, not the actual problem -- the fix is almost always checking the status code and looking at the raw response body first, rather than trying to debug the JSON parsing step itself.
questions.example:
response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
print(response.status_code)
print(response.text)  # look at the RAW body before calling .json()

if response.status_code == 200:
    data = response.json()
else:
    print('Request failed, not attempting to parse as JSON')
commonMistakes: Calling .json() without first checking the status code, then being confused by a decode error on an error response's HTML/text body
Not looking at the raw response.text to see what actually came back before assuming the parser is broken
Assuming an empty response body is valid JSON (it isn't)
Treating a JSON decode error as the root problem instead of a symptom of an earlier, unhandled failure
keyPoints: A JSON decode error usually means the response body simply wasn't valid JSON, often because the request actually failed
Check status_code and print the raw response.text before assuming the JSON parser itself is the problem
An error response's body is often HTML or plain text, not JSON
An empty response body also fails to parse as JSON

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the most likely root causes
Describes checking status code and raw text as the investigation step
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Diagnosing and fixing an overfitting model
questions.prompt: You train a classification model and get 99% accuracy on the training set, but only 68% on the validation set. Walk through how you'd confirm this is overfitting, and three concrete things you'd try to fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: The 99%-vs-68% gap between training and validation accuracy is itself the confirmation -- a model that has genuinely learned the underlying pattern performs comparably on both; a large gap specifically where training is high and validation is much lower is the signature of overfitting, meaning the model has memorized specifics of the training data (including its noise) rather than learning something that generalizes. Three concrete fixes: first, add regularization (like L2 weight penalties, or dropout for a neural network), which directly discourages the model from fitting the training data too precisely. Second, get or use more training data if possible, since a model has a harder time memorizing noise in a larger, more varied dataset than a small one. Third, reduce the model's capacity/complexity -- fewer parameters, a shallower tree, fewer layers -- since an overly complex model relative to the amount of data available is exactly what makes memorization possible in the first place. A fourth common option, simpler than all three, is reducing the number of training epochs or using early stopping once validation performance stops improving even as training performance keeps climbing.
questions.professionalAnswer: That gap is already the diagnosis -- a model that actually understood the pattern wouldn't do dramatically better on data it's already seen than on data it hasn't, so 99% versus 68% is a textbook overfitting signature, not something I'd need extensive further investigation to confirm. For fixes, I'd try them roughly in this order of effort: first, add regularization -- an L2 penalty or dropout, depending on the model type -- since that's often a small code change with a real effect. Second, if I'm using early stopping or a fixed number of epochs, I'd check whether validation accuracy actually peaked and started getting worse well before training finished, in which case just stopping earlier helps directly. Third, if the model has a lot of capacity relative to how much data I actually have, I'd simplify it -- fewer layers, fewer trees, fewer features -- since an overly powerful model relative to a small dataset is exactly the setup that makes memorization possible rather than forcing real generalization.
commonMistakes: Assuming a high training accuracy alone means the model is good, without checking validation accuracy at all
Responding to overfitting by making the model MORE complex, which usually worsens it
Not checking whether validation performance already peaked earlier in training (missed early-stopping opportunity)
Trying only one fix and giving up instead of combining regularization, data, and complexity adjustments
keyPoints: A large training-vs-validation accuracy gap, with training much higher, confirms overfitting
Regularization (L2, dropout) directly discourages memorizing training-data specifics
More/varied training data makes memorization harder
Reducing model complexity or using early stopping addresses excess capacity relative to the data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly confirms overfitting from the accuracy gap
Proposes at least three genuinely distinct, correct fixes
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: A dataset's missing values are breaking training
questions.prompt: You try to train a model on a customer dataset and scikit-learn raises an error about NaN values before training even starts. Beyond just dropping every row with a missing value, what are your realistic options, and how would you decide between them?
questions.modelAnswer: Most scikit-learn models can't handle NaN values directly and will raise an error rather than silently working around them, so the first step is identifying which columns actually have missing values and how much -- a column missing 2% of its values is a very different situation from one missing 60%. For a column with a small amount of missing data, imputation is usually reasonable: filling numeric columns with the mean or median (median is safer when the column has outliers, since the mean would be pulled by them), and filling categorical columns with the mode or an explicit 'Unknown' category. For a column missing a very large share of its values, imputing that much of it risks inventing a misleadingly strong signal out of mostly-guessed values, so dropping that entire column is often more honest than keeping it. Dropping individual rows with any missing value at all is the simplest option but can throw away a large, potentially non-random chunk of the dataset if missingness isn't spread evenly -- it should be a last resort, not the default.
questions.professionalAnswer: The error itself just tells me scikit-learn won't proceed with NaNs present, so my first real step is checking, column by column, how much is actually missing, rather than just reaching for a blanket drop-missing-rows call everywhere. If a numeric column is missing a small percentage, I'd impute with the median rather than the mean, since the median isn't dragged around by outliers the way the mean is. For a categorical column, I'd either impute the most common category or, often better, add an explicit 'Unknown' category, since sometimes the fact that a value is missing is itself meaningful information worth keeping rather than hiding. If a column is missing most of its values, I'd seriously consider dropping that column entirely instead of imputing the majority of it, since at that point I'd mostly be inventing data rather than filling in a few genuine gaps. I'd only drop entire rows as a last resort, and even then I'd first check whether the missingness is random or concentrated in a particular subgroup, since dropping rows non-randomly can quietly bias the remaining dataset.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to dropping every row with any missing value without checking how much data that actually discards
Imputing with the mean on a column that has significant outliers instead of the more robust median
Imputing a column that's missing the large majority of its values instead of considering dropping the column
Not checking whether missingness is random or concentrated in a subgroup before dropping rows
keyPoints: Check how much is missing per column before choosing a strategy -- a small gap and a mostly-empty column need different handling
Impute small gaps: median for numeric (robust to outliers), mode or 'Unknown' for categorical
Consider dropping an entire column that's missing the large majority of its values
Dropping rows should be a last resort, and only after checking the missingness isn't concentrated in a non-random subgroup

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames checking missingness extent per column first
Proposes sound imputation strategies with correct reasoning
Correctly treats row-dropping as a last resort with a caveat

questions.title: Choosing between a dataclass, a dict, and a plain class
questions.prompt: You're writing code that represents a parsed API response as a Python object with a handful of known fields. Would you reach for a dataclass, a plain dict, or a hand-written class with __init__, and what would make you choose differently?
questions.modelAnswer: A dict is the lightest option and fine for throwaway or highly dynamic data where the fields aren't fixed or known ahead of time, but it offers no attribute-style access, no built-in validation, and no protection against a typo in a key name, which only surfaces as a silent bug or a KeyError at runtime. A dataclass is usually the right default for a response with a known, fixed set of fields: the @dataclass decorator generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ automatically from a short list of typed field declarations, giving attribute access (response.content instead of response['content']), a readable repr for debugging, and type hints that tools can check, all with very little boilerplate. A hand-written class with a manual __init__ is worth the extra code only when you need real custom behavior beyond just holding data -- validation logic in __init__, computed properties, or methods that operate on the data -- since a dataclass can also have methods added to it, but once a class needs significant custom construction logic, writing __init__ explicitly makes that logic clearer than cramming it into a dataclass's more declarative style.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a parsed API response with known fields, I default to a dataclass almost every time: a short @dataclass block with typed field declarations for content, tokens_used, and model gives me attribute access, a useful repr for debugging, and equality comparison, all without writing __init__ by hand. I'd use a plain dict only if the fields genuinely aren't fixed or known ahead of time -- something more dynamic, like arbitrary metadata -- because the API's own structure is still evolving at the point I'm writing this code. I'd write a fully manual class with its own __init__ when I need real logic at construction time, like validating that tokens_used is non-negative or raising a clear error for a missing required field, since dataclasses support that too via __post_init__, but once that validation gets non-trivial, an explicit __init__ reads more clearly than a dataclass post-init hook doing a lot of work.
questions.example:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ChatResponse:
    content: str
    tokens_used: int
    model: str

resp = ChatResponse(content='Hi there', tokens_used=12, model='gpt-mini')
print(resp.content)  # attribute access, not resp['content']
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a dict for a response with a known, fixed shape, losing attribute access and type-checking for no real benefit
Writing a fully manual __init__ for a simple data holder that a dataclass would cover with far less code
Not realizing dataclasses can still have methods and custom __post_init__ validation added
Choosing a dict 'to keep it simple' and then accessing it with bracket indexing everywhere, which is more error-prone than it looks
keyPoints: dict: best for dynamic/unknown fields, but no attribute access or validation
dataclass: good default for a response with a known, fixed field set -- minimal boilerplate, attribute access, repr, equality
Manual class with __init__: worth it for genuine custom construction logic/validation beyond just holding data
Dataclasses can still have methods and custom validation, so they're not limited to pure data holding

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly characterizes all three options and their tradeoffs
Gives a sensible default recommendation with justification
Identifies when a manual class is genuinely warranted

questions.title: Choosing a branching strategy for a small team
questions.prompt: You're setting up Git workflow conventions for a 4-person team building an AI application together. Would you recommend a Git Flow-style strategy with long-lived develop/release branches, or a simpler trunk-based approach with short-lived feature branches off main? What would change your answer?
questions.modelAnswer: For a small, 4-person team, trunk-based development -- short-lived feature branches that branch off main, get reviewed quickly, and merge back within a day or two -- is almost always the better fit: Git Flow's additional long-lived branches (develop, release, hotfix) add real process overhead -- more branches to keep in sync, more merge points where things can drift -- that pays off mainly at a scale where multiple release versions genuinely need to be maintained in parallel, which a small team building one continuously-deployed application typically doesn't need. The deciding factor that would change the answer is whether the team needs to support multiple released versions simultaneously (for example, maintaining a stable production release while a next major version is developed separately) -- that's the scenario Git Flow's structure is actually built for, and a team in that situation benefits from the extra branches even at a small headcount.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a 4-person team, I'd recommend trunk-based: short-lived feature branches off main, a pull request and quick review, then merge back within a day or two, keeping main always close to deployable. Git Flow's extra branches -- develop, release, hotfix -- exist to solve a problem this team likely doesn't have yet: needing to maintain multiple released versions of the software at the same time. With 4 people shipping one continuously deployed application, that extra branch structure is mostly overhead -- more places for things to get out of sync, more process to remember -- without a corresponding benefit. The one thing that would flip my recommendation is if this team suddenly needed to support, say, an older stable release for some customers while actively developing a new major version for others -- that's genuinely the situation Git Flow's structure is designed around, and at that point the extra discipline becomes worth it even for a small team.
commonMistakes: Recommending Git Flow by default regardless of team size or actual release-management needs
Not identifying the real deciding factor -- supporting multiple released versions in parallel
Assuming trunk-based development means no code review or no branches at all, rather than short-lived ones
Treating this as a purely technical choice without considering the team's actual workflow and deployment cadence
keyPoints: Trunk-based development (short-lived branches off main) suits most small teams shipping one continuously deployed app
Git Flow's long-lived develop/release/hotfix branches solve a specific problem: maintaining multiple released versions in parallel
The deciding factor is whether multiple versions genuinely need parallel maintenance, not team size alone
Overhead from extra long-lived branches isn't justified without that parallel-version need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a clear, justified recommendation for this team's situation
Correctly characterizes what Git Flow's structure is actually for
Identifies the correct deciding factor that would change the answer

questions.title: Forking workflow vs. direct branch-and-PR workflow
questions.prompt: When would you use the forking workflow (each contributor forks the repo to their own account) instead of giving every contributor direct push access to branch off the main repository? What's actually different about the two, mechanically?
questions.modelAnswer: In the direct workflow, every contributor has push access to the same shared repository and creates branches directly inside it, opening pull requests from branch to branch within that one repo. In the forking workflow, a contributor doesn't have push access to the original repository at all -- they create their own independent copy (a fork) under their own account, push branches and commits to that fork, and open a pull request from their fork's branch back to the original repository, which the original repository's maintainers then choose to accept. The forking workflow exists specifically for situations where you can't or shouldn't give direct push access to every contributor: open-source projects accepting contributions from the general public being the classic case, since granting push access to an unknown, unvetted public contributor isn't reasonable, but a fork-and-PR contribution still gives the maintainers full review and control before anything merges. For a small internal team where everyone is already trusted and has legitimate reasons to push, the direct branch-and-PR workflow is simpler and has no real downside -- forking adds a layer of indirection with no corresponding benefit in that situation.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanical difference is about where the contributor's branch actually lives. In the direct model, I branch inside the same shared repository everyone already has push access to. In the forking model, I don't have push access to the original repo at all -- I create my own full copy of it under my own account, push my branch there, and then open a pull request from my fork back to the original repo, which its maintainers review and merge (or don't) entirely at their discretion. I'd reach for forking specifically for open-source-style situations -- contributing to a public project I don't work for, where it would be unreasonable for the maintainers to hand out push access to every random contributor. For an internal team of people who are already trusted collaborators, I'd skip forking entirely and just use direct branches off the shared repo with pull requests -- forking there is extra indirection with no real security or workflow benefit.
commonMistakes: Not understanding that forking creates an entirely separate copy of the repository under the contributor's own account
Using the forking workflow for a trusted internal team where it adds unnecessary indirection
Assuming a pull request from a fork works mechanically differently from a pull request between branches in the same repo, when the review/merge process is otherwise similar
Not identifying open-source/untrusted-contributor access control as the real reason forking exists
keyPoints: Direct workflow: contributors push branches directly to the shared repository
Forking workflow: contributors push to their own separate copy, then PR back to the original repo
Forking exists to let maintainers accept contributions without granting push access to untrusted/unknown contributors
For a trusted internal team, direct branching is simpler with no real downside

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the mechanical difference between the two workflows
Correctly identifies when forking is actually warranted
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Designing a simple API client class
questions.prompt: You need to call an AI provider's API from several different places in a small application. Would you write a single reusable client class that wraps the API, or just call requests directly wherever it's needed? What belongs inside that client class if you build one?
questions.modelAnswer: Calling requests directly in multiple places means the base URL, authentication header construction, error handling, and retry logic all get duplicated at every call site, which is both more code overall and a maintenance risk -- a change to how authentication works, or a new retry rule, has to be found and updated in every scattered location instead of one place. A single client class centralizes exactly that shared, repeated concern: it typically holds the base URL and API key in __init__, exposes clean methods for each actual operation (like a chat method rather than the caller constructing the full request), and internally handles building headers, checking the response status, raising a clear exception on failure, and retrying on transient errors -- so every call site gets that behavior automatically and consistently, rather than it being re-implemented, and potentially re-implemented inconsistently or with bugs, in multiple places.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I'm calling the same API from more than one place, I write a client class rather than repeating requests calls scattered around the codebase. I'd design it with __init__ storing the shared api_key and base_url config, then a method per actual operation -- a chat method or an embed method -- that internally builds the headers, makes the call, checks the status code, and raises a clear, specific exception on failure rather than letting a raw requests exception leak out. Centralizing retry logic and backoff inside the client is the other big win: if I later decide every call should retry twice with backoff on a 5xx, I change that in exactly one place instead of hunting down every call site in the application that happens to hit this API directly.
commonMistakes: Repeating requests calls with duplicated headers/base-URL logic at every call site instead of centralizing it
Not raising a clear, specific exception on failure, letting a raw requests exception leak out to every caller
Putting retry/backoff logic in each individual call site instead of inside the client class
Overengineering a client class with far more configurability than the application actually needs
keyPoints: Scattering direct API calls duplicates auth/error-handling/retry logic across the codebase
A client class centralizes base URL, auth, and shared behavior in one place via __init__
Expose clean, specific methods per operation rather than making callers build raw requests
Centralize retry/backoff and clear error-raising inside the client so every call site benefits consistently

Describes a sensible, correct client class design
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Streaming vs. a single blocking response
questions.prompt: Why do AI provider chat APIs commonly offer a streaming option, returning the response piece by piece, instead of only waiting and returning the full completion in one response? When would you choose streaming, and when would a single blocking call be better?
questions.modelAnswer: A streaming response sends the model's output incrementally, piece by piece, as it's generated, rather than making the caller wait for the entire response to finish generating before receiving anything at all. For a chat response that might take several seconds to fully generate, streaming lets an application start showing the user text immediately as it arrives, which feels dramatically faster and more responsive even though the total time to finish generating is the same either way -- this is purely a perceived-latency and user-experience improvement, not a speed improvement to the underlying generation itself. Streaming makes sense specifically when a human is waiting and watching the output appear, like a chat interface. A single blocking response is simpler to implement and is the better choice when the full response needs to be processed as one complete unit before anything useful can be done with it anyway -- for example, parsing the complete output as structured JSON, where a partial, still-arriving fragment isn't useful until the whole thing has arrived regardless of whether it streamed in or arrived all at once.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of streaming as solving a perceived-speed problem, not an actual-speed problem -- the model still takes the same total time to generate the whole response either way; streaming just lets the caller start seeing pieces of it immediately instead of waiting in silence for the whole thing to finish. That's exactly the right tradeoff for a chat UI where a person is sitting there watching text appear -- streaming makes it feel instant even though the full response isn't actually ready any sooner. I'd reach for a single blocking call instead whenever the response needs to be consumed as one complete unit before I can do anything useful with it -- if I'm asking for a JSON object back and parsing it, a half-arrived stream of JSON isn't valid or usable yet anyway, so blocking for the complete response is both simpler to code and loses nothing in that specific case.
commonMistakes: Assuming streaming makes the model generate the response faster overall, rather than just changing when pieces become visible
Using streaming for a case where the output must be parsed as one complete structured unit (like JSON) anyway
Adding the complexity of handling a stream when a simple blocking call would have worked fine for a non-interactive use case
Not recognizing streaming's benefit is specifically perceived latency for a human watching output appear
keyPoints: Streaming sends output incrementally as it's generated; it improves perceived latency, not total generation time
Streaming suits interactive, human-facing use cases like chat interfaces
A blocking call suits cases where the full response must be consumed as one complete unit (e.g., parsing structured JSON)
Streaming adds implementation complexity that isn't worth it for non-interactive use cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what streaming actually improves (perceived latency, not total time)
Gives a correct scenario favoring streaming
Gives a correct scenario favoring a blocking call

questions.title: Why an OpenAI-style chat API is shaped the way it is
questions.prompt: OpenAI-style chat completion APIs take a list of messages (each with a role like 'system', 'user', or 'assistant') rather than a single plain-text prompt string. Why is the API designed around a list of role-tagged messages, and what does that structure actually enable?
questions.modelAnswer: A single plain-text prompt string has no built-in way to distinguish who said what -- instructions from the application, versus what the end user typed, versus what the model itself said earlier in the conversation, would all have to be mashed into one string and separated with ad hoc formatting that the model has to interpret as best it can. The role-tagged message list makes that structure explicit and unambiguous: a 'system' message sets overall instructions/behavior for the assistant, 'user' messages are what the actual end user said, and 'assistant' messages are what the model itself said previously -- all passed back in on every call, since these APIs are stateless and don't remember prior turns on their own. That structure is what makes multi-turn conversation possible at all: each new call sends the entire message history back to the model, with roles intact, so the model can see exactly who said what, in what order, and respond appropriately to the latest user message with full context of everything that came before.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it through what it enables rather than just describing the format. Because each message carries an explicit role, the API can keep the system's instructions cleanly separate from what the user actually typed, instead of both being mashed into one undifferentiated block of text that the model has to parse out itself. That separation is also what makes a real multi-turn conversation possible: since the API itself is stateless and doesn't remember anything between calls, my application has to resend the entire conversation -- system message, every past user message, every past assistant reply -- on every single call, with roles intact, so the model can see the full context and know which parts were instructions, which were the human talking, and which were its own earlier replies.
commonMistakes: Assuming the API remembers prior conversation turns on its own instead of requiring the full message history to be resent every call
Not distinguishing the purpose of the 'system' role from 'user' and 'assistant'
Mashing instructions and user input into one message instead of using the system role to separate them
Forgetting to include prior assistant replies in the message list, losing conversational context
keyPoints: Role-tagged messages (system/user/assistant) explicitly separate instructions, user input, and prior model output
These APIs are stateless -- the full message history must be resent on every call
The system role sets overall assistant behavior/instructions, kept separate from user content
This structure is what makes genuine multi-turn conversation possible

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the purpose of role-tagged messages
Correctly explains statelessness and resending full history
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What a function/tool calling schema is for
questions.prompt: At a basic level, what is a 'function calling' or 'tool calling' schema when working with an AI provider's API, and what problem does it actually solve?
questions.modelAnswer: A function/tool calling schema is a JSON description of a function your own application has -- its name, a plain-language description of what it does, and the names/types of the parameters it needs -- that you send along with your request so the model knows this capability exists and can be used. It solves the problem of getting a model's free-text output turned into something a program can reliably act on: instead of asking a model to 'respond in a way I can parse' and hoping its plain-text answer happens to be in a usable format, you describe a specific function (like a get_weather function taking a city string) and the model, when it determines that function is relevant to the user's request, responds with a structured, well-formed call to that function -- naming it and filling in argument values -- rather than a plain English sentence that your code would then have to try to parse. Your application is still responsible for actually executing that function and running the real code; the model itself only decides when to call it and what arguments to call it with, it doesn't execute anything on its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it as giving the model a menu of things it's allowed to ask for, described in a structured way it can understand: here's a function called get_weather, it needs a city as a string parameter, here's what it does in plain language. When a user asks something that function is relevant to, instead of the model trying to answer in free text and hoping I can somehow parse a city name back out of a sentence, it responds with a structured call that I can directly plug into my own actual get_weather function. The important thing I'd clarify for someone newer to this: the model never runs the function itself; it only decides that calling it would help and fills in the arguments. My code still has to actually execute get_weather and, usually, send the result back to the model in a follow-up call so it can use that real data in its final answer to the user.
commonMistakes: Assuming the model actually executes the function itself instead of just deciding to call it and filling in arguments
Not providing a clear, specific description for the function, leading the model to call it incorrectly or not recognize when it's relevant
Confusing a tool/function schema with the actual implementation -- the schema just describes the function's interface, your code still implements it
Expecting the model to always call the right function with no need to handle the case where it calls something unexpected or malformed
keyPoints: A function/tool schema is a JSON description of a function's name, purpose, and parameters sent to the model
It solves the problem of turning a model's output into a structured, program-usable call instead of free text
The model only decides to call a function and fills in arguments -- it never executes the function itself
Your application is responsible for actually running the function and typically returning its result to the model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a function/tool schema contains
Correctly explains the problem it solves (structured vs. free-text output)
Correctly clarifies the model doesn't execute the function itself

questions.title: What's actually happening during an LLM API call
questions.prompt: At a conceptual level -- no deep math required -- walk through what actually happens between sending a prompt to an LLM API and receiving the response back. What are the major stages?
questions.modelAnswer: At a conceptual level there are a few major stages. First, tokenization: the input text (your prompt, plus any conversation history and system instructions) is broken into tokens, the model's actual unit of processing, by the specific tokenizer paired with that model. Second, the model itself -- already trained, with its parameters fixed -- processes that sequence of tokens in a forward pass, which is pure inference, not training; nothing about the model's underlying parameters changes from answering your request. Third, generation: the model produces its response one token at a time, where at each step it computes a probability distribution over all possible next tokens and samples one (with some randomness, controlled by a setting commonly called temperature), then feeds that chosen token back in as part of the input for choosing the next one, repeating until it decides to stop or hits a length limit. Finally, those generated tokens are converted back into readable text (detokenized) and returned to you as the response, and the whole thing is billed based on the token counts involved in both the prompt sent and the response generated.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as four steps without getting into the actual math. My prompt and any conversation history first get tokenized -- chopped into the model's token units by its specific tokenizer. That token sequence goes through the already-trained model in what's called inference -- importantly, this is not training; the model's parameters are completely fixed at this point, inference is purely using what it already learned, not updating it. The model then generates its reply one token at a time: for each next token, it computes a probability distribution over everything it could say next and picks one, feeds that choice back in, and repeats -- which is also why the exact same prompt can produce slightly different wording run to run, since that choice has some randomness built in. Finally, the generated tokens get turned back into readable text and sent back as the response. The part I'd specifically flag for someone newer to this is the training/inference distinction -- an API call is never training the model on your data in that moment, it's using a model that was already fully trained beforehand.
commonMistakes: Assuming an API call trains or updates the model on your specific input
Not knowing generation happens one token at a time, each depending on the ones generated before it
Thinking the model picks a single deterministic 'best' response instead of sampling from a probability distribution
Skipping the tokenization/detokenization steps as if the model reads and writes plain text directly
keyPoints: Tokenization converts input text into the model's token units before any processing
The model's forward pass during an API call is inference, not training -- parameters don't change
Generation happens one token at a time, sampling from a probability distribution at each step
Generated tokens are detokenized back into readable text for the response

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes tokenization as the first stage
Correctly distinguishes inference from training
Correctly describes token-by-token generation

questions.title: Using a pretrained model as-is vs. fine-tuning it
questions.prompt: You need a model to perform a specific classification task for your company's data. How would you decide between using a pretrained model exactly as it is versus fine-tuning it on your own data, at a basic beginner level of understanding?
questions.modelAnswer: Using a pretrained model as-is means relying entirely on what it already learned from its original, general training data, with no further training on your specific data at all -- this is the simplest, fastest, and cheapest option, and it's often surprisingly effective, especially for fairly general tasks the model was likely already exposed to plenty of similar examples of during its original training. Fine-tuning means continuing to train that already-pretrained model further, specifically on your own labeled data, which lets it adapt to patterns, vocabulary, or categories that are specific to your exact task and wouldn't have been well represented in its original general training. The basic decision test: try the pretrained model as-is first, since it costs little to attempt, and only invest in fine-tuning (which requires your own labeled dataset, more time, and more cost) if the as-is model's performance on your actual task genuinely isn't good enough, or if your task uses highly specific categories, vocabulary, or patterns that a general-purpose pretrained model is unlikely to have learned well.
questions.professionalAnswer: My default move is always try it as-is first, because that costs almost nothing -- no labeled dataset of my own needed, no training time, just load it and test it against real examples from my actual task. I'd only move to fine-tuning if that as-is test genuinely falls short, usually in one of two ways: the task uses vocabulary or categories specific enough to my company's data that a general-purpose pretrained model was unlikely to have seen much like it during its original training, or the as-is accuracy is measurably too low for the task to actually be useful as it stands. Fine-tuning is a real investment -- it needs a labeled dataset of my own task's examples, more time, and more compute cost -- so I treat it as the fallback once I've concretely established the simpler option isn't good enough, not the default starting point.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to fine-tuning without first testing how well the pretrained model performs as-is
Not recognizing fine-tuning requires your own labeled dataset, which as-is use doesn't need at all
Assuming fine-tuning is always better, ignoring that it costs real time, data, and compute for a benefit that may not be needed
Not considering whether the task's vocabulary/categories are specific enough to actually require fine-tuning
keyPoints: Using as-is relies entirely on the model's original general training -- fast, cheap, often effective
Fine-tuning continues training on your own labeled data to adapt to task-specific patterns
Decision test: try as-is first; fine-tune only if performance genuinely falls short or the task is highly specific
Fine-tuning requires your own labeled dataset and real additional time/cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the difference between as-is and fine-tuning
Gives a sensible decision test (try as-is first)
Correctly identifies fine-tuning's real costs/requirements

questions.title: Choosing a pretrained model using its model card
questions.prompt: You're browsing a model repository and find three pretrained models that all claim to do the task you need. What would you actually look at on each model's model card to decide between them?
questions.modelAnswer: A model card is documentation published alongside a pretrained model describing what it actually is, and the things most worth checking before choosing one include: what data it was actually trained on, since a model trained on data very different from your real use case (different domain, different language, different style of text) often performs worse in practice than its benchmark numbers alone would suggest; its reported performance/benchmark metrics, ideally on a task similar to yours, understanding that benchmark numbers from the model's own card can be optimistic and worth verifying on your own real examples before fully committing; its size (parameter count), which affects how much compute/memory it needs to run and how fast it responds, since a larger model isn't automatically better for your use case if a smaller one already performs well enough and runs cheaper and faster; and its license, since a model that scores well but can't actually be legally used for your intended purpose, commercial or otherwise, isn't a real option no matter how good its benchmarks look.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work through the model card systematically rather than just looking at a headline accuracy number. First, what was it trained on -- if it's a sentiment model trained mostly on product reviews and I need it for medical text, that mismatch matters more than a benchmark score from a totally different domain would suggest. Second, I'd look at its actual reported performance on a task similar to mine, while remembering that's the model author's own benchmark, so I'd still test it against a handful of my own real examples before trusting it outright. Third, size -- a bigger model with marginally better benchmarks isn't worth it if it costs noticeably more to run and a smaller one already clears the bar I actually need for this task. And I always check the license last but non-negotiably, because if I can't legally use a model the way I intend to -- commercially, for instance -- none of its other qualities matter at all.
commonMistakes: Choosing based on headline accuracy alone without checking what the model was actually trained on
Ignoring the license, which can make an otherwise great model unusable for the intended purpose
Assuming a larger model is automatically better without weighing cost/speed against actual need
Trusting the model card's own benchmark numbers without testing against real examples from the actual use case
keyPoints: Check what data the model was trained on for a domain/style match with the real use case
Check reported performance on a similar task, but verify with your own real examples
Check model size against actual compute/cost/speed needs -- bigger isn't automatically better
Check the license to confirm it's actually usable for the intended purpose

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies training data relevance as a key factor
Identifies performance verification beyond the headline benchmark
Identifies size/cost tradeoffs
Identifies license as a non-negotiable check
